newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CS Research cuts estimate for Nestle.
newsitem.headline: CS Research cuts estimate for Nestle.

text.p: CS Investment Research said it had cut its earnings forecast for Nestle SA in 1996 and 1997 because it now felt coffee sales would not meet CS's previous estimate of three percent volume growth.
In a research note, it put 1996 estimated earnings per share at 84.3 Swiss francs, down from its original target of 86.5, and cut its 1997 estimate to 91.1 francs from 91.9.

It estimated first-half net profit, which it and other analysts said will be reported on Friday, at 1,395 million Swiss francs. Nestle posted a net profit of 1,118 million in the first six months of 1995.

"Few first-half estimates are available yet, but there appears to be no consensus," CS analyst James Amoroso said. "Two major brokers also have a first-half net income of around 1.4 billion francs, but two other major brokers have estimates of 1.2 billion to 1.25 billion (plus 10 percent)."
It suggested investors buy on net profit above 1.4 billion, hold if between 1.3 and 1.4 billion, reduce if between 1.2 and 1.3 billion and sell if less than 1.2 billion.
A Nestle spokeswoman would not confirm it would release its first-half profit figures on Friday, but reiterated the report was expected in mid-September.
Nestle said in July that first-half sales rose 5.8 percent and confirmed it expected good net profit growth for the year.
Sluggish sales in major coffee markets are weighing on profit growth, analysts agree. This is especially true in the United States, Nestle's second-largest coffee market.

"There is a general maturing of coffee as a drink because the main consumers are older people who are dying off and younger people are not drinking as much," said one analyst who did not want to be named.
Nestle also faces the challenge of matching strong growth at rival Swiss companies in other sectors, especially chemicals, said David Sheridan at James Capel in London.
"We are modestly positive on Nestle," he said, forecasting annual earnings growth of 13.5 percent over the next three years. But this was no reason to accumulate the stock aggressively.
"We have a 'hold' recommendation but a kind of weak hold," he said, adding Nestle would probably not outperform the overall Swiss market.
"Novartis (to be created by the merger of Ciba-Geigy AG and Sandoz AG ) and Roche have steady rates of good growth. It is hard for other sectors to do well against that pair," he said.
He saw Nestle's full-year 1996 net profit rising 14.8 percent to 3,350 million Swiss francs, of which half or even more could be posted in the first half.
